title: Week 35 · Lesson 59: Hepatology & Viral Hepatitis Pharmacology — HBV, HCV, DILI & FNP Safety
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 35 — Lesson 59: Hepatology & Viral Hepatitis Pharmacology — HBV, HCV, DILI & FNP Safety

FNP-level goal: Use liver-focused clinical reasoning to select and monitor medications safely, recognize viral-hepatitis care needs, prevent avoidable hepatotoxicity and interactions, and rapidly escalate jaundice, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, or other signs of decompensated liver disease.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain how liver disease can alter medication metabolism, exposure, and adverse-effect risk.
  • Differentiate acute versus chronic hepatitis B and the broad goals of HBV management.
  • Describe the role of direct-acting antivirals in HCV treatment and why interaction review matters.
  • Recognize drug-induced liver injury, hepatic decompensation, and acute liver-failure red flags.
  • Apply safe monitoring, alcohol/supplement counseling, vaccination, co-infection, pregnancy, and referral principles.
  • Coordinate care rather than independently stopping high-stakes HBV/HIV or HCV therapy.

Part 1 — The Liver Is a Medication-Safety Organ

The liver metabolizes many medications, produces proteins involved in coagulation, handles bilirubin, and contributes to energy, nutrient, and immune functions. Liver disease can change medication exposure, bleeding risk, protein binding, tolerance of adverse effects, and the reliability of laboratory interpretation. A normal dose for one patient may be unsafe or ineffective for another with impaired hepatic function.

Before prescribing in liver disease, identify the diagnosis and stage when known, current symptoms, bilirubin and synthetic-function concerns, kidney function, alcohol exposure, current medicines and supplements, hepatitis status, pregnancy considerations, and the clinician managing the liver disease. Do not use an isolated transaminase result as the whole liver assessment.

Part 2 — Pattern Recognition: Hepatocellular, Cholestatic, and Synthetic Dysfunction

A liver-injury pattern may be predominantly hepatocellular, cholestatic, mixed, or related to impaired synthetic function. Symptoms and signs can include fatigue, nausea, right-upper-quadrant discomfort, jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools, edema, bruising, ascites, confusion, or gastrointestinal bleeding. The pattern, time course, medication exposure, alcohol use, viral risk, obstruction risk, and hemodynamics shape the differential.

Do not assume abnormal liver tests are due to a new medication, nor assume a patient with normal early tests is safe. Evaluate the clinical picture, trend, and red flags. Suspected severe injury requires urgent assessment and a medication/supplement review rather than a delayed repeat lab alone.

Part 3 — Drug-Induced Liver Injury: Think Timeline and Alternatives

Drug-induced liver injury can occur with prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, supplements, herbals, alcohol, and illicit substances. The FNP must establish all exposures, start dates, dose changes, intermittent use, prior tolerance, and symptom onset. Ask about acetaminophen-containing combination products, weight-loss products, bodybuilding products, traditional remedies, and concentrated supplements specifically.

Do not automatically attribute all hepatitis to medication. Viral hepatitis, autoimmune disease, ischemia, biliary obstruction, metabolic liver disease, infection, and malignancy may mimic DILI. When a potentially hepatotoxic medicine is suspected, assess severity and consult the responsible prescriber or urgent care pathway before stopping a medication that is essential or has withdrawal/rebound consequences.

Part 4 — Acute Hepatitis B and Chronic Hepatitis B Are Different

Acute HBV infection is generally managed with supportive care, with hospitalization or specialist care when severe. Chronic HBV is a long-term condition in which treatment decisions depend on viral activity, liver inflammation and fibrosis, comorbidities, pregnancy, co-infections, and the individual patient. Not every person with chronic HBV needs antiviral medication, but everyone needs appropriate longitudinal assessment.

Chronic HBV care includes liver monitoring, counseling to limit alcohol, review of medications and supplements, testing and prevention for co-infections as appropriate, vaccination against hepatitis A when indicated, and surveillance/referral according to current guidance. Patients with chronic HBV should be cared for with clinicians experienced in its management.

Part 5 — HBV Medication Safety and Reactivation

Some therapies used for HBV suppress viral replication rather than cure infection, and treatment can be long term. Never tell a patient to stop HBV-active medication because they feel better, have a mild side effect, or need a new prescription without reviewing the full clinical context. Stopping or changing HBV-active therapy can create serious risk in selected patients.

HBV reactivation is particularly relevant with immune-modulating therapy, cancer treatment, transplant-related therapy, and HIV treatment changes. Before starting significant immunosuppression or modifying an HIV regimen, identify HBV status and coordinate with hepatology, infectious disease, oncology, rheumatology, or the appropriate specialty team.

Part 6 — HCV Is Curable, But Treatment Is Not Casual

Modern direct-acting antiviral therapy can cure more than 95% of HCV cases with short, oral treatment courses in many patients. Curative treatment should be considered for essentially everyone with detectable HCV RNA unless a specific exception applies. Before treatment, however, the patient needs a full evaluation for chronic liver disease, medication interactions, HBV and HIV status, pregnancy considerations, and appropriate follow-up.

Do not equate a positive antibody test with active HCV requiring treatment; confirmation of current infection and clinical evaluation matter. Do not treat a successful course as the end of liver care for patients with advanced fibrosis, cirrhosis, ongoing exposure risk, or other liver disease.

Part 7 — DAA Interactions Can Change Outcomes

Direct-acting antiviral regimens can interact with acid-reducing agents, cardiovascular medicines, antiepileptics, tuberculosis therapies, antiretrovirals, supplements, and other commonly used drugs. Some interactions reduce antiviral effectiveness; others increase toxicity of the antiviral or the concurrent drug. A medication that was safe before HCV treatment may need review before the first DAA dose.

Reconcile every medicine, including nonprescription products and supplements, before and during HCV treatment. Use a current interaction resource and communicate with the treating HCV clinician or pharmacist. Do not ask a patient to stop an essential cardiac, seizure, psychiatric, HIV, or transplant medicine without a coordinated alternative plan.

Part 8 — HBV/HCV/HIV Coinfection Requires Deliberate Coordination

Coinfection can affect medication selection, timing, monitoring, and reactivation risk. In people with HIV/HBV coinfection, changes to an ART regimen can change HBV activity; discontinuing agents active against HBV can cause serious hepatocellular injury from reactivation hepatitis. In people starting HCV treatment, HBV status matters because reactivation can occur in the appropriate clinical context.

The FNP should recognize the issue, verify all active infections and therapies, avoid unilateral medication changes, and involve experienced HIV/hepatitis care. Co-infection is a situation where “simplifying the medication list” can unintentionally create harm.

Part 9 — Cirrhosis and Decompensation Change the Threshold

Patients with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis may have altered drug handling and increased risk of ascites, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy, infection, kidney injury, and hepatocellular carcinoma. New confusion, sleep-wake reversal, asterixis, jaundice, increasing abdominal girth, edema, hematemesis, melena, fever, renal decline, or hypotension can signal decompensation or another serious complication.

Do not manage suspected decompensation with routine outpatient reassurance. Assess ABCs, vital signs, mental status, bleeding, infection, volume status, and medication exposure. Arrange emergency care for instability, gastrointestinal bleeding, significant encephalopathy, sepsis concern, or rapidly worsening symptoms.

Part 10 — Alcohol, Acetaminophen, Supplements, and Metabolic Health

Alcohol can worsen liver injury and complicate medication safety. Ask about quantity, pattern, withdrawal risk, and readiness for change without stigma. Acetaminophen-containing products are common and may be duplicated unintentionally. Supplements can be hepatotoxic, contaminated, or interactive even when marketed as natural or liver-supporting.

Metabolic risk also matters. Weight, diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, nutrition, activity, and sleep affect liver and cardiovascular health. Counseling should be realistic, culturally respectful, and paired with treatment for alcohol use disorder, nutrition support, or behavioral health when desired.

Part 11 — Pregnancy, Prevention, and Household Care

Pregnancy changes testing, medication, and perinatal-prevention decisions for viral hepatitis. Ask about pregnancy intention before starting or renewing relevant therapies and coordinate promptly with obstetric and hepatitis specialists when pregnancy is possible or confirmed. Do not assume every antiviral or supplement has the same reproductive safety profile.

Prevention includes hepatitis A and B vaccination as appropriate, harm-reduction services, testing and treatment of co-infections, and counseling about blood exposure. Household and sexual contacts may have their own testing or vaccination needs under current public-health guidance.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: New Jaundice After a Medication Change

A patient develops fatigue, dark urine, pruritus, and yellowing of the eyes two weeks after a new medication and supplement were started. They also report several drinks most evenings.

FNP reasoning: assess severity and urgent red flags, obtain a complete exposure timeline, and evaluate hepatocellular injury, cholestasis, obstruction, viral hepatitis, and other causes. Do not simply advise stopping one product and rechecking labs later if jaundice or systemic symptoms are present. Arrange timely evaluation and coordinate changes to essential medications.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: HCV Treatment and a New Reflux Medication

A patient beginning an HCV direct-acting antiviral asks to start an over-the-counter acid-reducing product for reflux.

FNP reasoning: identify the exact DAA regimen and product, check a current interaction resource, and coordinate with the HCV clinician or pharmacist. The answer depends on the regimen and cannot be assumed from the words “acid medicine.”

Part 14 — Clinical Case: HIV/HBV Regimen Change

A patient with HIV and chronic HBV asks to stop part of their ART because they are tired of taking multiple medicines.

FNP reasoning: validate the burden while recognizing that some ART components may also suppress HBV. Do not advise a partial stop. Review adherence barriers, confirm the full regimen and viral-hepatitis status, and urgently coordinate with HIV/hepatitis care to create a safe alternative plan.

FNP Liver and Viral-Hepatitis Medication-Safety Framework

  1. Define the liver problem: symptoms, injury pattern, function, timeline, stage of disease, and red flags.
  2. Reconcile all exposures: prescriptions, over-the-counter products, acetaminophen combinations, supplements, alcohol, and substances.
  3. Identify infections: clarify HBV, HCV, HIV, and relevant co-infection status before high-stakes medication changes.
  4. Check interactions: use current drug-specific resources before adding DAA, ART, immunosuppression, or other significant medication.
  5. Coordinate: involve hepatitis, HIV, pharmacy, oncology, rheumatology, or obstetric care when treatment or reactivation risk is complex.
  6. Escalate: send suspected acute liver failure, decompensation, major bleeding, severe jaundice, encephalopathy, or instability for urgent/emergency evaluation.

High-Yield Summary

Liver disease: can change medication exposure, bleeding risk, and toxicity; interpret the patient, not one laboratory value.
DILI: requires a complete exposure timeline and differential, not an assumption that one new drug is the only cause.
Chronic HBV: needs expert longitudinal care; treatment and interruptions require careful coordination.
HCV: is curable in most cases with DAAs, but medication interaction and liver-stage assessment are essential.
Coinfection: makes unilateral ART/HBV/HCV changes dangerous because reactivation and interaction risks may be present.
Cirrhosis: lowers the threshold for urgent escalation with confusion, bleeding, infection, jaundice, ascites, or renal decline.
FNP standard: protect the liver by reconciling all exposures, checking interactions, coordinating specialist care, and recognizing decompensation early.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Hepatitis testing, antiviral selection, treatment duration, monitoring, medication interruption, DILI evaluation, pregnancy care, HCC surveillance, and emergency triage must follow current CDC/AASLD/IDSA guidance, product labeling, local policy, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
